messages.subject: blocked split-plot anova
parts:
Hello, 

I'm trying to analyse a blocked split plot design in lme4 or nlme and would like some help in making sure I am using the correct code.

The design I have is a blocked split-plot design with repeated measures so I have 2 between-plot and 2 within-plot effects.
There are 3 random blocks on the landscape with two fences in each block. Each fence is split and has either a winter warming (WW) or no winter warming (WC). On either side of the fence there are 4 sub-plots, 2 of which have a summer warming treatment (SW) and 2 of which have no summer warming (SC). Every sub-plot is monitored once a year for 5 years. The question is whether carbon flux changes significantly between treatments and through time. 

It looks like this:

3 blocks replicated on the landscape, random between-subject effect 
2 fences nested in each block, this is the unit of replication for my fixed between-subject effect WW described below, these are coded 1-6 so that each fence in each block has a unique ID
1 treatment applied to each fence, either WW or WC, fixed between- subject effect
1 treatment crossed with each treatment at the fence level, either SW or SC, these are applied in 2 sub-plots per fence, fixed within-subject effect
this produces WWxSW, WWxSC, WCxSW and WCxSC treatments
each sub-plot is monitored once per year for 5 years, fixed within-subject effect

I want to make sure my variables are coded correctly. Currently each fence is unique 1:6, blocks are A,B,C and sub-plots are 1:8, repeated in every block/fence combination. This makes sense to me, the fences and blocks are unique; plot 1 in every block/fence comes from the same treatment and, if treatment has an effect, they should behave similarly regardless of where they are on the landscape. I think this way block/fence will be my unit of replication for the WW effect and sub-plot my unit of replication for repeated measures in years. 

Here is my code attempt: 

model.nlme <- lme (carbon ~ WW*SW*year,
                      random=~1|block/fence/WW/SW/sub-plot, 
                    data = flux.cum.treat.plot,method="REML")

anova(model.nlme)
            numDF denDF   F-value p-value
(Intercept)     1   188  94.03039  <.0001
WW              1     5   1.94065  0.2224
SW              1    10   0.19706  0.6666
year            1   188 190.17488  <.0001
WW:SW           1    10   0.95409  0.3517
WW:year         1   188   5.20715  0.0236
SW:year         1   188   0.07169  0.7892
WW:SW:year      1   188   1.33104  0.2501

Is this correct?
One thing that is a little puzzling to me is why year has only 1DF? Shouldn't it be 4? 

However, this does not work in lmer. Why? 

model <- lmer(carbon ~ WW*SW*year +     # these are my fixed effects, WW is between-subject and SW, year are within-subject
                 (1|block/fence/WW/SW/year/sub-plot),
               data = flux.cum.treat.plot)
Error in checkNlevels(reTrms$flist, n = n, control) : 
  number of levels of each grouping factor must be < number of observations


I know that lme4 is the more favoured package, I started using nlme because I want to be able to define the covariance structure as autoregressive (AR1), which I do not think lme4 can do. But why does nlme accept sub-plot as a nested factor and lme4 does not?

Does the hierarchy of fixed or random effects matter, as long as the order of nesting is correct? If I have my fixed effect in the y ~ x + z part of the formula, will it always be considered fixed?

I have read some suggestions that it is good coding practice to have a different data column for the main and nested variable, even if they are identical. In my case that would be eg: WW_fixed, WW_nested. Is this purely for coding clarity?

Thanks very much for any help,
Marguerite


*********
This questions is quite similar to Emily Peffer's post from some time ago:
ANOVA with nested random and fixed effects: help! 
The biggest difference is that my largest unit of observation, the block, is random, so are block/fence and sub-plot. Based on the discussion in that thread, I think my model.nlme should be right.
